name: Phone neck habit change

card.summary: Changing how you hold and look at your phone to reduce 'text neck'; research links the posture to neck pain, but nothing tests facial or neck asymmetry.
card.aka: Text neck habit change, tech neck
card.note: Text neck studies are mostly cross-sectional surveys; causation and appearance effects are not established.

quick.overview:
Text neck is the term for the head-down, flexed-neck posture adopted while using phones and tablets. Phone neck habit change refers to altering that behaviour, for example how long and in what posture devices are used, in the hope of reducing neck strain and, in looksmaxxing framing, neck asymmetry.

Published work on text neck concerns neck pain and posture, mostly in surveys and biomechanical models. None has measured effects on neck or facial asymmetry.
quick.mechanism: Biomechanical modelling shows neck flexion loads the cervical spine joints. Observational studies associate text neck posture and heavy phone use with neck pain in adolescents and young adults, though the link is not uniform.
quick.risks: Behaviour change itself carries little risk. The evidence base is mainly cross-sectional, so cause and effect, and whether altering habits changes appearance, are unestablished.

lead: Phone neck habit change means altering how people hold and look at phones, tablets and laptops so that the head and neck spend less time in a sustained forward-flexed position. The posture is popularly called text neck, and a related lay term, iHunch, describes a forward head carriage with rounded upper back associated with heavy device use [1][2][11]. In looksmaxxing discussion the goal is a more upright head-and-neck line, better-looking neck and jaw profile, and less neck or upper-body asymmetry, reached by setting devices at eye level, taking breaks and strengthening the neck and upper back.

Researchers have studied text neck in children, adolescents, university students and adults, generally reporting associations between text-neck posture or heavy device use and neck pain, while noting that most work is cross-sectional and that causation is still being worked out [1][3][4][5][6][7]. Biomechanical modelling has quantified how much load flexion places on the cervical spine joints [8]. Neck pain itself is common, affecting around two-thirds of people at some point in life according to general references [12].

The chain people describe runs from device habits to head and shoulder posture to how the neck, jaw line and upper back look in profile. Published studies have examined the first link (device use and posture or pain); none has measured effects on facial or neck asymmetry or on appearance.
infobox: Sustained neck flexion with phones and screens
Mostly cross-sectional surveys, models, case reports

paras: A review of text neck syndrome in children and adolescents describes new technologies shifting neck pain prevalence toward younger ages, and links early and inappropriate use of computers and especially mobile phones to a cluster of symptoms called text neck syndrome [1]. A 2022 review characterises it as a new epidemic needing disentangling, other papers describe it as an adverse postural phenomenon, and a 2017 commentary in The Spine Journal asks whether it should be called an epidemic at all [2][9][10].

The term iHunch is used for a related picture: the head carried forward of the shoulders with the chin poking out and the upper back rounded. A Wikipedia entry on the topic traces the earliest dated use to a 2013 Radio New Zealand segment and attributes to a 2014 study by Hansraj the widely repeated figure that load on the neck rises several-fold as the head tilts forward [11].

sections.h: Posture, appearance and the looksmaxxing angle
paras: Forward head carriage changes the profile view: the ear sits ahead of the shoulder line, the chin and jaw can look less defined, and the upper back can look rounded. This is why posture work is discussed alongside neck training and jaw-line improvement in appearance communities. Practitioners describe the habit change in general terms: raising screens toward eye level, bringing the phone up instead of lowering the head, alternating hands and sides, taking regular breaks, and combining this with neck and upper-back strengthening [11].

A Wikipedia overview of neck pain notes that for posture-related neck pain the treatment is usually corrective, such as aligning the shoulders over the hips and ergonomic changes, and that research is growing into embedded warning systems that alert people to poor device posture [12]. Exercise, including specific strengthening, and motor-control exercises are listed there as helpful for neck disorders [12].

A modelling study of eight healthy men quantified intervertebral joint loads through the cervical spine in flexion while accounting for muscle activation, noting that flexion is a recognised mechanical risk factor for chronic neck pain [8].

A cross-sectional study of 150 young adults aged 18 to 21 in Rio de Janeiro investigated whether text neck was associated with neck pain [3]. A 2021 study in the journal Spine examined the association between text neck and neck pain in adults [4]. A study of university students in Saudi Arabia during the COVID-19 pandemic examined text neck posture, smartphone addiction and neck disorders [5], and a 2023 paper examined musculoskeletal symptoms from phone and backpack postures in school-aged children [6].

A 2022 case report described preventing progression of text neck in a young man [7]. Reviews highlight that the evidence is largely observational and that findings are not uniform across ages [1][2][10]. No studies found testing whether changing phone habits alters neck or facial asymmetry or appearance.

Phone posture is discussed as part of a broader posture and neck-line routine, usually alongside neck training and jaw exercises. No community threads are cited here, so specific claims are not attributed.
